hello.note: For anyone, at any time. Goddag (go-DAY) is more formal

how-are-you.note: The h in hv is silent

im-well.note: The d in godt is silent

good-night.note: Only when parting at night. Good evening is godaften (go-AF-ten)

goodbye.note: Hej hej (hai hai) is the everyday goodbye

please.note: Formal and rarely used. Danes say tak at the end instead: En kaffe, tak (a coffee, thanks)

thank-you.note: Mange tak (MANG-e tahk) means thank you very much. Danes say tak constantly

youre-welcome.note: Literally "thanks yourself", the answer to tak

no.note: Nej tak (nai tahk) is no, thank you

excuse-me.note: Sorry, and excuse me to get attention or get past

my-name.note: dh is a soft d, almost like the th in "this". The audio uses Peter as the example name

your-name.note: Danes say du, you, to everyone, even strangers and bosses

where-from.note: Answer Jeg kommer fra... (yai KOM-er fra), I come from...

speak-english.note: Nearly every Dane speaks excellent English, but a few words of Danish are always appreciated

thousand.note: Prices are in kroner (KROH-ner), written kr. or DKK. Danish tens are famously odd: 50 is halvtreds (hal-TRES)

hundred-thousand.note: Written 100.000: Denmark marks thousands with a dot

would-like.note: The polite way to order. Even simpler: just the thing and tak. The audio uses en kaffe (een KAF-fe), a coffee
would-like.spoken: Jeg vil gerne have en kaffe

i-want.note: Literally "I'll take...", the natural way in a shop. The audio uses den her (den heer), this one

do-you-have.note: I (ee) is "you all", the usual way to ask a shop. The audio uses vand (van), water

too-expensive.note: Denmark is expensive for everyone, Danes included

discount.note: Prices are fixed in shops; bargaining only at flea markets (loppemarked)

card.note: Cards and phones are accepted almost everywhere, and some places take no cash at all

bill.note: Service is included in the price, so tipping is optional

taxi.text: Kan du ringe efter en taxa?
taxi.say: kan doo RING-e EF-ter een TAK-sa
taxi.note: Taxis are expensive. Cycling is how Danes get around: bikes are easy to rent

airport.note: Copenhagen Airport is Kastrup, 15 minutes from the centre by metro or train

train-station.note: The main station, such as Københavns Hovedbanegård in Copenhagen

which-train.note: The audio uses Aarhus (OR-hoos), Denmark's second city, as the example

buy-ticket.text: Hvor kan jeg købe en billet?
buy-ticket.say: vor kan yai KUR-be een bi-LET
buy-ticket.note: Tickets are mostly bought in the DSB or Rejsebillet apps

two-tickets.note: The audio uses Aarhus as the example

trip-length.text: Hvor lang tid tager det til...?
trip-length.say: vor lang teedh tar deh til ...
trip-length.note: The audio uses Aarhus as the example
trip-length.spoken: Hvor lang tid tager det til Aarhus?
trip-length.filled: Hvor lang tid tager det til ⟦Aarhus⟧?

delicious.note: Also Det smager godt! (deh SMAA-er GOT), it tastes good

allergic.note: Add the food: nødder (NUR-dher) nuts, jordnødder (YOR-nur-dher) peanuts, skaldyr (SKAL-dewr) shellfish. The audio uses nuts
allergic.spoken: Jeg er allergisk over for nødder

what-called.note: Point at the dish or item

table-for-two.note: For more people: til tre (treh), 3, or til fire (FEER-e), 4

recommend.note: Try smørrebrød, open sandwiches on rye bread, at lunch

coffee.note: Danes drink a lot of it, ideally with something sweet and a dose of hygge

water.note: Tap water is excellent. Danskvand (DANSK-van) is sparkling water

hot.note: Hot, and warm. Spicy is stærk (stairk)

cheers.note: Look each person in the eye as you raise your glass

help.note: Shout it. For police, ambulance or fire, call 112

need-doctor.text: Jeg har brug for en læge
need-doctor.say: yai har BROO for een LAY-e
need-doctor.note: For an ambulance, call 112. In Copenhagen, call 1813 for urgent medical advice

pharmacy.note: Look for the green Apotek sign
